shared_text:
The flight. A regional jet taking off from a large airport and climbing out on a published departure procedure. Visual conditions, daytime.

The crew. The captain was the pilot flying and the first officer the pilot monitoring. The captain had about 5,800 hours.

What happened. Before departure the first officer completed the flows in full, and the checklists were done as usual, without time pressure. The take-off was normal, with the usual speed callouts. During the climb-out the aircraft encountered wake turbulence. At 1,000 ft above the ground the captain called for the navigation modes, and soon afterwards the crew changed to the departure frequency. The crew normally relied on the automation to manage speed on departure, and expected the flight director to command the correct speed. Soon after the frequency change, the crew noticed that the aircraft was not accelerating as expected. ATC asked for maximum forward speed, and then gave a heading off the departure route because of the slow speed. The crew discussed possible causes aloud. The first officer then saw that the speed selector was in manual mode instead of the FMS mode used for departure. It had been in manual mode since before take-off. The crew selected FMS speed, and the aircraft accelerated to 210 knots.
safe_outcome: Shortly afterwards the aircraft resumed the departure route. There was no conflict with other traffic. No one was hurt and the aircraft was not damaged.
bad_outcome: Another aircraft was climbing nearby. Both crews received TCAS resolution advisories and followed them, and the aircraft passed about 300 feet vertically and half a mile apart. A flight attendant on this aircraft was thrown against a galley cart during the manoeuvre and received a minor injury.
notes: Removed under rule 3: the captain's 'neglected to select', 'accidentally' and 'I will be more careful next time'; the first officer's later reflections that radio calls and wake turbulence slowed their response, 'complacency and lack of experience', 'this mistake', future self-checks, the first officer's own briefing habit as pilot flying, and the general remark that most pilots switch to FMS speed after landing and the switch is rarely out of position (afterwards commentary; the crew's expectation at the time, that the automation would manage speed, is kept). Kept: the first officer's statement that flows and checklists were done as usual without time pressure; the wake turbulence, radio frequency change and ATC's speed request and heading, all received before the cause was found. The switch position since take-off is stated as a fact confirmed afterwards. Moved under rule 5: resuming the departure route. Removed under rule 6: airport, runway and departure procedure names. Judgement calls: the two narratives differ slightly in order; the captain's order (ATC request and heading before the discussion) is followed. Standard safe-ending line used: the wake encounter and ATC's heading are not reported as a traffic conflict. Bracket 'climbing': the event is in the departure climb, where the natural conflict is another departing aircraft.
